findings.finding: The fallback `git ls-remote --tags origin` makes the hook's decision depend on a network call inside a synchronous PreToolUse hook. findings.finding: Fail-open on any exception (`Any exception: allow`) silently disables the guard. A regression in the lexer/decision code (e.g., an unhandled payload shape from a future Claude Code version) means the "prevent before" net F1a/F1b/F4 is gone with no signal.

findings.finding: Command substitution is not handled: `$(git push origin main)` or backtick forms slip through the lexer (`shlex` + splitting on `&& || ; | &`). Similarly a push hidden in `sh -c "git push --tags"` or `make push` is invisible. This is inherent to Bash-matcher hooks, but the full-run report showed models improvise command forms.
findings.suggestion: Accept the limitation, but note it in the registry row and LEARNINGS so the campaign doesn't over-trust the hook as the sole net (it explicitly sits under F1a/F1b/F4 code paths, which is the right layering).

findings.finding: The 48-hour staleness window means a genuinely long-running release (paused >48h, then resumed) is silently allowed through. Combined with ls-remote fallback this creates two independent "allow" paths that don't cross-check each other.
findings.suggestion: Cheap improvement: if the state file exists but is stale AND the record for HEAD is missing, still require the ls-remote check before allowing (i.e., staleness downgrades "deny" to "check remote", never to unconditional allow).

findings.finding: Trunk detection by fixed names (main/master/develop) plus "no refspec or HEAD on a trunk branch" will miss trunk-adjacent branches (e.g., `release/`, `hotfix/`) that the skill's release flow may actually push. If the skill's own flow pushes a release branch, the guard blocks the skill's own recovery commands (e.g., finishing a partially-completed release).

findings.finding: The mini-plan's Files list and test list look complete (hooks.json entry, two scripts, three test files, registry row, LEARNINGS/FINDINGS), but it doesn't mention the doc obligation trigger: the deny output is a user-visible message, so per the spec's own rule ("guide only if a user-visible message is introduced") the diff may owe a guide mention, not just the registry row.

findings.finding: The lexer/decision split with an `Action` dataclass is the right amount of structure for the matching complexity required (heredocs, redirects, `-C`, Windows paths) — this is not over-produced. findings.suggestion: No change; affirming the design shape. findings.finding: The plan accepts a record for an ancestor of HEAD when intervening commits contain only events. The specification explicitly requires a record for current HEAD and says a record for a different commit must block.
findings.suggestion: Require exact HEAD equality. If P4’s event commits make that impossible, STRICT-STOP for an operator decision on the producer/consumer contract before implementing the exception.

findings.finding: An `ls-remote` error allows the action. A network outage, authentication failure, or missing `origin` therefore bypasses the guard precisely when an active release has no valid record. The blanket “any exception: allow” creates the same bypass for internal failures.
findings.suggestion: Once an active release and protected action are established, deny if record validation cannot complete. Keep malformed tool input and inactive releases separate from errors validating an active release.

findings.finding: The 48-hour expiry, remote-tag completion check, and environment-variable bypass introduce exemptions absent from the supplied specification. An interrupted release can remain incomplete beyond 48 hours, and a published tag does not establish that subsequent merge or release-page actions have the required record.
findings.suggestion: Use the existing producer’s documented release lifecycle to determine activity. Remove these exemptions unless the referenced operator decisions explicitly authorize them; otherwise STRICT-STOP. Removing the remote lookup also avoids network latency on protected tool calls.

findings.finding: Hard-coding `main`, `master`, and `develop` does not identify the repository’s actual trunk. The matcher can miss a custom trunk or a push such as `git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<trunk>`, while treating an unrelated `develop` branch as protected.
findings.suggestion: Resolve trunk using the project’s established configuration and classify refspec destinations, including explicit `HEAD:<trunk>` forms. Add focused tests for custom trunk names and source-to-destination refspecs.

findings.finding: The plan does not establish that command execution context and state lookup stay aligned. `git -C` changes the target repository, while `gh --repo` can target another project; resolving state solely from the hook’s cwd can validate the wrong release or falsely block another project.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the action’s target before locating release state, following existing repository conventions. Test `-C` from outside the project and explicit GitHub repository selection. If cross-repository targeting has no defined policy, obtain the required operator decision.  The hook is a suitable mechanism, but the proposed decision logic weakens the explicit HEAD requirement and introduces unsupported ways to bypass an active release guard. This assessment uses the supplied specification and mini-plan; local file inspection was blocked by execution policy.  SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise
